item.title: SAP confirms suspicious activity; GitHub, Project Granite and token theft reported; no customer-data access found
item.description: SAP told dpa and BleepingComputer on 2026-11-26 and 2026-11-27 that it identified suspicious activity, took measures to protect customers and has found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data; a letter that dpa saw in part places the activity in SAP's GitHub developer platform. DER SPIEGEL's insider reports, without SAP's confirmation, stolen employee authentication tokens and copied and possibly modified source code, and heise, relaying Handelsblatt's company circles, reports restricted GitHub access, paused development workflows and replaced signing keys. SAP has not said how the attackers got in, who they are, or whether any software delivered to customers or any signing key customers verify is affected.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

SAP: suspicious activity in its GitHub development platform (Project Granite), with reports that employee authentication tokens were stolen and source code copied or modified; SAP says it found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data and has not said whether any delivered software is affected

SAP told BleepingComputer and dpa that it identified suspicious activity, promptly took the necessary measures to protect its customers, and found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data on the investigation to date; it gave no vector, actor, discovery date or list of affected systems (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27; tagesschau.de, 2026-11-27; Handelsblatt, 2026-11-27). A letter that dpa saw in part places the activity within SAP's platform for developer productivity and software delivery on GitHub and asks staff to check whether they must change credentials (translated from German) (tagesschau.de, 2026-11-27). Handelsblatt, citing company circles, says SAP detected the incident the week before and that software development was attacked (translated from German) (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-27).

Reported by media from internal sources and not confirmed by SAP: DER SPIEGEL's insider says the attacker stole authentication tokens of SAP employees and used them to copy and also modify SAP source code on GitHub, and that the attackers may have had help from AI systems; heise, relaying Handelsblatt, reports that SAP restricted access to GitHub, stopped automated processes in software development and replaced signing keys; BleepingComputer, Handelsblatt and heise add that, according to SPIEGEL, SAP tracks the incident internally as Project Granite, a name SAP has not confirmed (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27; DER SPIEGEL, 2026-11-26; heise online, 2026-11-27; Handelsblatt, 2026-11-27). SecurityWeek notes that none of the reports indicate tampered code reached software delivered to SAP customers, and WirtschaftsWoche that SAP has left open whether customers must act (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-27; WirtschaftsWoche, 2026-11-27). SAP is part of the Swiss public sector's estate: the Federal Audit Office says the federal administration runs SAP R/3, supported until the end of 2027 and being replaced with S/4HANA, and Inside IT reports an existing S/4HANA landscape in the canton of Zurich's administration; no Swiss impact is reported (EFK, 2023-05-10; Inside IT, 2026-11-27).

Exposure
Organisations that consume SAP-delivered code, packages or updates, or verify SAP signatures; SAP has said nothing on which artifacts or keys are in scope, and no source says delivered software is affected (SecurityWeek, 2026-11-27).
Detection
The reported behaviour is use of stolen employee tokens against a source-control platform; for SAP customers the observable is on their side of the boundary, namely the provenance of SAP-delivered artifacts and any signing-key change in SAP's own communications.
Defender takeaway
SAP customers should watch SAP's own security communications for which artifacts or signing keys are in scope and verify any key change through SAP's channel; no customer action has been published, and SAP declined to say whether customers pulling SAP code from GitHub should act (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-27). For your own pipelines, 1Password disclosed on 2026-11-25 an intrusion through an employee's corporate GitHub account (1Password, 2026-11-25); review how employee tokens reach source control and CI.

Builds on: 1Password breach via an employee GitHub account exported customer records; vaults not affected

item.title: Hunt.io: crew staged a Swiss tax office's AD database via ntdsutil IFM; fake JDBC driver loader; edge exploit kit
item.description: Hunt.io recovered three exposed attacker directories and reports a domain-controller workflow against "a Swiss tax office": a log of ntdsutil install-from-media creation and a script that copies the Active Directory database and registry hives from a controller share to staging, decodes them and requests removal of the media. Complete off-host transfer is not confirmed, the victim is unnamed and the report does not show how access was gained. The kit also holds a Java loader registered as a Microsoft SQL Server JDBC driver, Apollo- and Poseidon-derived implants, a commercial employee-monitoring product used as a command channel and staged exploits for edge services that Hunt.io says show availability, not success; it assesses a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking, Southeast Asia-based crew and names no group.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Hunt.io: exposed attacker directories show a crew staging a Swiss tax office's domain-controller database through ntdsutil install-from-media, a Java loader posing as the SQL Server JDBC driver and an exploit kit for edge services; the Swiss victim is unnamed, the access route is not shown and complete transfer is unconfirmed

Hunt.io recovered the contents of three exposed open directories and, reading the operators' own files, reports a domain-controller workflow against a Swiss tax office: a log records ntdsutil install-from-media creation, and a script copies the domain database and the registry hives from a controller share to a staging area, decodes them with a single-byte XOR and then requests removal of the install-from-media set (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Hunt.io says complete off-host transfer is not independently confirmed, that an NTLM-relay run against an internal LDAP service belongs to the same environment, and that the Swiss output begins after code execution was already available, so how the crew first got in is not shown (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). The report names no canton, commune or federal body, and Hunt.io says it notified CISA before publishing (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).

The same files hold a Java class registered as a java.sql.Driver service provider that poses as Microsoft's SQL Server JDBC driver: its boot routine runs when an application loads the JAR, with no scheduled task needed, and either polls an HTTPS endpoint on TCP 8443 for commands passed to cmd.exe or decodes a packed file into an Apollo-derived Windows executable written under the Java temp directory and started from Java (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Hunt.io also describes a Poseidon-derived Linux implant behind a server labelled Mythic, a commercial employee-monitoring product whose agents the operators drive with custom clients, and a reconnaissance stage that sends base64-encoded output in chunks inside GET request paths; it says the artifacts show a Poseidon-derived build, which does not establish that it ran on an external victim, and an Apollo derivation with no verified runtime command-and-control configuration (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Staged exploits cover edge and remote-access services, among them Citrix NetScaler (CVE-2025-5777), FreePBX (CVE-2025-57819) and PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), and Hunt.io states that their presence establishes availability, not successful operation against any named target (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25). Hunt.io reads the operation as a Chinese-speaking, Southeast Asia-based cybercrime crew running a Russian-authored toolkit and ties it to no named group and no state sponsor (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
Active Directory domain controllers and Java application servers that load third-party JARs; Hunt.io's other victims are a US hospital system, a US manufacturer and a Bangladeshi university; law firms and US federal agencies are mainly reconnaissance targets, and one law firm was attacked without success (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).
Detection
On domain controllers, ntdsutil install-from-media creation that no administrator requested, followed by reads of the database and the SYSTEM and SECURITY hive copies from the share by another host and a removal of the media; NTLM relay and coercion activity against domain controllers; on Java application servers, a JAR whose service-provider descriptor names a com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc class that matches no vendor build, java writing an executable under the temp directory and then starting a child process, and HTTPS polling from application servers to TCP 8443; in proxy logs, GET paths carrying long base64 chunks (Hunt.io, 2026-11-25).
Defender takeaway
Hunt domain controllers for install-from-media creation and share-staged copies of the directory database and hives, and enforce SMB signing and LDAP channel binding, which Hunt.io names as the hardening against the relay and coercion tooling; review Java servers for unexpected JDBC providers, and treat the Swiss victim claim as a single-source reading of recovered files until a Swiss body or the victim comments.

item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:57 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelheadlinesummaryaffected_productsentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6, 3.21.11, 3.20.13 and 3.19.17 (2026-11-22) carry the Ruby fix and GitLab's 2026-11-25 release backports it to five older branches, so Veria Labs' table, unchanged since 2026-11-21, is stale; Veria's announced Rails exploit was not found released on 2026-11-27, and a co-discoverer says a plain Rails app is exploitable.

GitHub's release notes list the Ruby update as a critical fix in GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.21.11 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.20.13 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) and 3.19.17 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), all dated 2026-11-22, with application-level mitigations where an update was not immediately possible; they name no Ruby version or CVE. GitLab's release of 2026-11-25 backports the Ruby fix, a bump to Ruby 3.3.14 and 3.4.13, to 19.3.10, 19.2.11, 19.1.11, 19.0.12 and 18.11.15, which it calls an exception to its maintenance policy (GitLab, 2026-11-25).

Veria Labs' Rails proof of concept was announced for 2026-11-25 or later; its page, blog feed and GitHub organisation show no release as of 2026-11-27, which does not show that no exploit exists. Sanft writes that Rack's multipart method override and a field charset reach the vulnerable case conversion in a plain Rails application, and that OpenAI sent the Ruby maintainers working exploit proofs for the case-conversion and an integer-overflow flaw on 2026-11-07; the second flaw is limited to Rack 3.2.1 and earlier (Durendal, 2026-11-19).

Open finding: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14: seven memory-safety flaws in the regexp engine and string case conversion, three rated Critical by the project, with proofs of concept for code execution; Veria Labs says Rails and classic Sinatra are exposed by default and announces a public Rails exploit for 25 November 2026 (CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 3.1 7.4) →

item.title: Update: Zammad 6.5.5 emergency-fixes the exploited session-leak RCE on 6.5; 7.2.3 now supersedes 7.2.2 (root escalation)
item.description: DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning an unencrypted database link and forging administrator session tokens, took credentials from Zammad's database, and kept cloud OAuth access after network isolation. The alert fired 7 h 21 min before a volunteer looked at it and 19 h 23 min before the CISO was informed; containment finished 27 h 41 min after it.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:56 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbodyupdated_at

DIVD's forensic report of 2026-11-25 says the attacker likely used ARTEX and moved from the Zammad host to Jira and Confluence by ARP poisoning an unencrypted database link and forging administrator session tokens, took credentials from Zammad's database, and kept cloud OAuth access after network isolation. The alert fired 7 h 21 min before a volunteer looked at it and 19 h 23 min before the CISO was informed; containment finished 27 h 41 min after it.

DIVD published the forensic report on its September breach on 2026-11-25 (DIVD CSIRT blog, 2026-11-25), written by Merlon Security with NVISO's analysis of the Google Workspace side. It says the attacker likely used ARTEX, on the basis of 990 scripts and 3,259 output files, scripts commented in an LLM style, an API token named artex- plus a number and a Zammad administrator account named artex.ops, ARTEX strings in an e-mail subject and the numeric job IDs that ARTEX's intents use; it names no actor (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The chain at behaviour level: the attacker probed the perimeter from 07:40 UTC on 2026-09-21; an administrator logged in to Zammad at 18:53 and the WebSocket flaw yielded that session cookie 1.3 seconds later; the replayed session wrote a file through the package-upload endpoint at 19:06 and a malicious Ruby mail template as an override of a mailer view at 19:27, which a user-creation request rendered, giving code execution as the zammad user at 19:27:58. Command and control ran through a Zammad API endpoint, with files staged in the web-served directory and fetched back through the egress proxy because direct outbound traffic was blocked. Root followed through the second flaw: a service that runs as root read configuration from a directory the zammad account owned, and a dropped file plus a kill of the web worker, which the supervisor restarted, gave root by 19:46 and left a setuid copy of bash (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

From the Zammad host, in the same web-application VLAN as Jira and Confluence, the attacker sniffed passively from 21:19 and from about 01:37 on 2026-09-22 ran ARP-poisoning scripts, reaching a man-in-the-middle position between Confluence and its PostgreSQL database at 02:27. The link was unencrypted, so it read the database protocol, learned the schema from captured traffic and injected its own SQL into live connections, writing a remember-me session token of its choosing for an administrator into Confluence's token table and presenting it at 08:49; Jira followed through its OAuth tables and a replay of remember-me tokens at 14:08. The report says TLS on the database links would have stopped the injection, asks for deny-by-default micro-segmentation inside the VLAN and says a containerised Zammad would have prevented the root step (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Persistence was a new Zammad administrator account and API tokens, a root-run systemd loop with Restart=always and cron entries that run text files dropped in the web-served directory, and an edit of Zammad's Google sign-in initializer that switched the access type to offline and added the Gmail scope, which captured nothing because no user signed in while it was live. Credentials taken included the hosting provider's mailbox password in cleartext, OAuth tokens for the two shared mailboxes, the database password, an Elastic credential and Jira's OAuth consumer private key and password hashes. NVISO says the content of the two shared mailboxes up to the credential and session resets must be considered potentially compromised, and that tokens were re-issued after the network isolation, so network isolation alone does not revoke cloud OAuth access (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

The alert fired at 19:43 UTC on 2026-09-21. A volunteer first looked at it at 03:04 on 09-22, 7 h 21 min later; the CISO was informed at 15:06, 19 h 23 min after the alert; and isolation completed at 23:24, 27 h 41 min after it (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Contradiction: DIVD's case page says "it took us 19 hours to initiate our first response on 22 September 2026" (DIVD, 2026-11-25), while the report says "The first response to these alerts was observed on Sep 22nd 2026 at 03:04 UTC", 7 h 21 min after the alert, and puts the CISO notification at 15:06 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24). The case page's own metrics table lists a mean time to acknowledge of 07:20:51 ("Time between first alert and SOC pickup") and a mean time to respond of 19:16:51 ("Time between first attack and formal response"), the same 7 h 21 min the report gives for the first look and about the 19 hours of the prose, so the two documents use "first response" for different intervals (DIVD, 2026-11-25). The report counts about 39 hours of actor interaction in the cloud, to 08:33 on 2026-09-23 (DIVD CSIRT, 2026-11-24).

Open finding: CVE-2026-102489 / CVE-2026-102490, Zammad helpdesk: a session-hijack remote code execution and a zammad-to-root escalation, both reported exploited since 21 September; 7.2.2 fixes the root flaw on DEB and RPM installs →

item.title: Update: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names six users
item.description: Wiz shows that ARTEX writes a numeric intent ID from a per-installation counter it does not reset by default, and Cairn a per-project one, into AWS and Azure resource names, session names and comments, a pivot for hunting and linking activity; Wiz ties ARTEX-Harvester to more than a dozen organisations, Huntback's exposed console shows a Global Administrator takeover at a South Korean university, and DIVD's forensic report finds the same numbering in its own breach.
item.content:encoded:
Update27 Nov 2026 04:54 UTCrun 2026-11-27T0355Z-intelsummaryentitiessourcesevidencesourcing_notebodyupdated_at

Wiz shows that ARTEX writes a numeric intent ID from a per-installation counter it does not reset by default, and Cairn a per-project one, into AWS and Azure resource names, session names and comments, a pivot for hunting and linking activity; Wiz ties ARTEX-Harvester to more than a dozen organisations, Huntback's exposed console shows a Global Administrator takeover at a South Korean university, and DIVD's forensic report finds the same numbering in its own breach.

Wiz Research shows how ARTEX and Cairn leak their intent numbering into victim logs. ARTEX draws intents, facts, findings, hints and digests from one counter per installation that is never reset by default, so intent numbers climb across runs and targets and consecutive ones are rare, and it puts the number in its working directory, its session name and its prompt; Cairn formats zero-padded counters per object type and resets them for every project (Wiz, 2026-11-25). The numbers surface wherever an API takes a name or comment: AWS role session names, SSM command comments, KMS key descriptions and aliases, security-group rule descriptions, Azure run-command, VM and app-registration names, and the error message of a denied call (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Wiz uses them to link activity across rotating residential-proxy addresses and victims, to separate installations and to read scope from a jump far larger than the activity in one victim's logs, and cautions that hits are tool markers and pacing clues, not operator fingerprints: unrelated installations collide in the same ranges and operators reset or parallelise (Wiz, 2026-11-25). Google's report of 2026-10-31 had already seen incremental numeric markers in ARTEX file names, account names, passwords and e-mail subjects without being able to explain them (GTIG and Mandiant, 2026-10-31).

Wiz's account of ARTEX-Harvester ties it, at varying confidence, to activity at more than a dozen organisations between late October and mid-November, clustered by a distinctive boto3 build, the cross-victim intent counter and proxy-pool overlap, and warns that activity labelled ARTEX comes from multiple unrelated operators; these two posts do not mention Storm-0940 (Wiz, 2026-11-23).

Huntback reads an exposed ARTEX console whose workspace holds a South Korean university, where the numbering also leaks onto the victim, with a local administrator account named after an intent number. Single sign-on accepted a stored password hash as the password, a Microsoft 365 password-reset bridge ignored the old password, and a password-grant token, which involves no browser and no second factor, carried Global Administrator from 18:47:53 UTC on 2026-11-16; student-style accounts were then created and licensed and a further account was made Global Administrator (Huntback, 2026-11-24). Huntback says a Conditional Access policy requiring multi-factor authentication for every user and blocking legacy and non-interactive password sign-ins would have stopped the token request, names no actor, and says its detection queries were not run against a live workspace (Huntback, 2026-11-24).

DIVD's forensic report on its own September breach says the attacker was likely using ARTEX and that ARTEX's intents are numeric job IDs included in all input and output (DIVD, 2026-11-24).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: Update: GeoServer RCE chain: public PoC, CISA lists two flaws as exploited; update to 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7
item.description: watchTowr reports exploitation attempts against the GeoServer chain, in the form of error-based probes that create and invoke stored queries, and NCSC Switzerland rates the chain actively exploited; watchTowr is the only observer and the sources name different CVEs as exploited. The record also adds CVE-2026-120704, the SQLite JDBC extension-loading step that Eye Security's variant of the chain uses.
item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagssectorscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbodyupdated_at

watchTowr reports exploitation attempts against the GeoServer chain, in the form of error-based probes that create and invoke stored queries, and NCSC Switzerland rates the chain actively exploited; watchTowr is the only observer and the sources name different CVEs as exploited. The record also adds CVE-2026-120704, the SQLite JDBC extension-loading step that Eye Security's variant of the chain uses.

watchTowr reports that attackers are exploiting the chain: its vulnerability FAQ of 2026-11-25 says the flaws are being exploited in the wild, and The Hacker News quotes watchTowr that attackers sent error-based exploit probes that create and invoke stored queries to check whether a server is vulnerable (watchTowr, 2026-11-25; The Hacker News, 2026-11-25). The sources disagree on which flaws: The Hacker News names CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 in its lead and CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129244 in its quote of watchTowr, watchTowr's prose names all five chain CVEs, and its own table then marked only CVE-2026-129245 as exploited. NCSC Switzerland's advisory 13242 of 2026-11-25 rates the chain Actively Exploited with a proof of concept available, labels only CVE-2026-120705 as actively exploited and lists watchTowr's post as its source (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-25). No victim, actor or scale is named; the project's own pages make no exploitation statement.

Eye Security's disclosure uses a different last step, CVE-2026-120704, administrator-controlled loading of an SQLite JDBC extension that gives native code execution and is fixed in the same three releases (Eye Security, 2026-11-24); on Windows the project says the extension library can load from an SMB share, so nothing needs staging on the server (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). CVE-2026-120705 echoes file contents only when a layer is published to anonymous users, and its fix reaches embedders through GeoTools 35.2, 34.6 and 33.7 (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). On a cluster, set the same GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY on every node, because the fixed releases generate a new random remember-me key at each start (watchTowr, 2026-11-25).

Open finding: GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7: a five-step chain from an anonymous WFS request to code execution (CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129243, CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129245, CVE-2026-129242) works on a default installation, was disclosed in advisories published on 2026-11-23 and has a public proof of concept; CISA lists CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 as exploited, and watchTowr reports exploitation attempts, which NCSC Switzerland relays as actively exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.2 for the critical step) →

item.content:encoded:
Update26 Nov 2026 05:05 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-intelheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencebodyupdated_at

Microsoft's defender guide of 2026-11-25 names six ARTEX users, adding the North Korean clusters Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet and the clusters Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, says ThreatBook sells an ARTEX Pro, and lists web-server, identity and egress detections; ThreatBook's own release presents the commercial edition as its product, which GTIG's fork description does not state.

Microsoft's defender guide of 2026-11-25 says it has observed state-sponsored and financially motivated actors such as Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon integrating ARTEX into their tooling (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). For Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet the basis is Microsoft's report of 2026-10-29, which says it has identified both using ARTEX since late October 2026 and says that human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives (Microsoft, 2026-10-29); the guide gives no campaign detail for Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, which The Record describes as Chinese state-backed groups (The Record, 2026-11-25). The Record also reports that The New York Times and Nextgov said ARTEX was allegedly used in attacks on the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (The Record, 2026-11-25). Nextgov, citing people familiar with the matter, says ARTEX is believed to have been used in the breach of an unclassified CIA and ODNI system for analyzing public and commercially available information and in an intrusion into the Defense Department's Cyber Defense Command, which one of its sources called low-impact, and that it is unclear who carried out the CIA and ODNI breach or whether information was taken (Nextgov, 2026-11-24).

Microsoft says ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November and began offering commercial access to an ARTEX Pro (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). ThreatBook's own launch release of 2026-10-16 already lists Artex Pro as an extension of the open-source Artex, developed as a personal project by the product lead of its RedAgents platform, and says the open-source edition was converted to closed source on 8 October 2026 after attackers misused it (Macau Business, 2026-10-16); GTIG lists ARTEX PRO among community forks, whereas ThreatBook's release presents it as the vendor's own extension, so the sources differ on whether it is a fork.

Microsoft says ARTEX can drive virtually any model, including open-weight and guardrail-stripped ones, and can switch models when one fails, so its activity is not necessarily constrained by any single provider's safety controls or visible in any single provider's telemetry; it adds that ARTEX introduces no new techniques and does not obfuscate by default, and calls behavior the most durable signal: a wide variety of requests in a brief time, retries of technique variants and next-stage actions at machine speed (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). Its detections, by telemetry class: on web servers, web-server processes (w3wp.exe, php-fpm, httpd or apache2, Java application servers) starting shells, script files created in web-accessible or upload directories, including files a database server process writes after its log file was pointed at a web directory, several short-lived web shells with incrementing names, and rapid reads of /etc/shadow, .env files, private keys and cloud credential files; in access logs, a client requesting 100 or more distinct paths with 50 or more client errors in one minute; in Entra sign-in logs, one address attempting service-principal sign-ins for three or more applications within an hour with both failures and successes, where a success after an invalid or expired client secret error warrants immediate investigation; in the audit log, one identity adding application credentials and assigning roles or permissions within an hour, and in one case an application assigning itself Global Administrator; and on egress, reverse shells and requests from servers to webhook and file-sharing services, where Microsoft's lever is to restrict outbound connections from web servers (Microsoft, 2026-11-25).

Microsoft's thresholds are defaults to tune: exclude build and automation servers that run shells under Java or Node.js, review file names because content management system updates also write script files, and do not alert on default curl, Wget, Python or headless Chromium user agents alone (Microsoft, 2026-11-25). Service-principal sign-ins are logged separately from interactive ones, so an empty hunt proves nothing where they are not collected (Microsoft, 2026-11-25).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

item.title: GeoServer RCE chain: public PoC, CISA lists two flaws as exploited; update to 3.0.2, 2.28.6 or 2.27.7
item.description: The GeoServer project published a batch of security advisories on 2026-11-23, most for flaws fixed in 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7, and five of them chain an anonymous WFS request to code execution: a path disclosure, a service-security bypass with a prefixed service name, an XML injection, a predictable remember-me key that forges an administrator session (critical, CVSS 4.0 9.2) and a JDBC deserialization. The reporter, who says it works on a default installation, published a full-chain proof of concept the same day; the project announced the fixed releases on 2026-10-19. CISA added CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-27 on evidence of active exploitation it does not describe, watchTowr reports exploitation attempts in the form of error-based probes that create and invoke stored queries, and NCSC Switzerland rates the chain actively exploited.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-129244 +5exploitedupdatedNATOA2

GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7: a five-step chain from an anonymous WFS request to code execution (CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129243, CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129245, CVE-2026-129242) works on a default installation, was disclosed in advisories published on 2026-11-23 and has a public proof of concept; CISA lists CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 as exploited, and watchTowr reports exploitation attempts, which NCSC Switzerland relays as actively exploited (CVSS 4.0 9.2 for the critical step)

The GeoServer project published a batch of security advisories on 2026-11-23, most for flaws fixed in 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7, which the project had announced on 2026-10-19 as an important upgrade for production systems (GeoServer, 2026-11-23; GeoServer, 2026-10-19). Five chain, in the order the project gives: a WFS stored-query exception that discloses the data directory path (CVE-2026-129244), service-security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS so anonymous users can create stored queries (CVE-2026-129243), an unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection (CVE-2026-120705), a predictable remember-me key that allows administrator session forgery (CVE-2026-129245, critical) and deserialization in the JDBC user and role services (CVE-2026-129242, administrator required) (GeoServer, 2026-11-23; GeoServer, 2026-11-23). The project says the critical advisory was first reported as step 4 of an unauthenticated remote command execution chain and that each step was given its own CVE at the CVE Numbering Authority's request (GeoServer, 2026-11-23).

The reporter says the chain gives unauthenticated remote command execution on a default installation: the service-name bypass lets an anonymous stored query read the files that hold the remember-me key and an administrator password digest, which forges an administrator session (CryptoCat, 2026-11-23). A full-chain proof of concept has been public since the reporter's write-up. Affected are 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5 and 2.27.6 and earlier, with 3.0.2, 2.28.6 and 2.27.7 as the fixed releases (GeoServer, 2026-11-23); the project says the 2.27 series has reached end of life (GeoServer, 2026-10-19). CISA lists CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 as exploited, and watchTowr reports exploitation attempts, which NCSC Switzerland rated actively exploited on 2026-11-25 (CISA, 2026-11-27; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-25).

Exposure
GeoServer on the affected builds with WFS reachable by anonymous users and the REST API reachable; the reporter says it works on a default installation, with the stock admin account enabled in the default user service and, for its payload, a Linux host, and that the chain read the live key, so it never depended on the shipped value and a rotated key alone does not close it (CryptoCat, 2026-11-23); the fixed releases use a random per-node key and invalidate existing remember-me cookies on upgrade (GeoServer, 2026-11-23).
Detection
In web access logs, WFS requests whose service parameter contains a slash such as x/WFS, and stored queries you did not create under the data directory's wfs/query and workspaces/*/wfs/query folders (GeoServer, 2026-11-23); in REST access logs, an administrator session that uploads a database file and creates a JDBC user group service (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). If exposure is suspected the project advises changing administrator passwords, because changing the key does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals it (GeoServer, 2026-11-23).
Defender takeaway
Update internet-reachable GeoServer to a fixed release now rather than at the next cycle, since a public full-chain proof of concept exists, CISA lists two of the chain's flaws as exploited and the fixes are weeks old; where it must wait, apply the project's workarounds for steps 2 and 4, and on any instance that ran an older build while reachable, review the stored-query folders and the administrator accounts.
Update26 Nov 2026 05:06 UTCrun 2026-11-26T0356Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagssectorscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteclassificationactionsbodyupdated_at

watchTowr reports that attackers are exploiting the chain: its vulnerability FAQ of 2026-11-25 says the flaws are being exploited in the wild, and The Hacker News quotes watchTowr that attackers sent error-based exploit probes that create and invoke stored queries to check whether a server is vulnerable (watchTowr, 2026-11-25; The Hacker News, 2026-11-25). The sources disagree on which flaws: The Hacker News names CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243 in its lead and CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129244 in its quote of watchTowr, watchTowr's prose names all five chain CVEs, and its own table then marked only CVE-2026-129245 as exploited. NCSC Switzerland's advisory 13242 of 2026-11-25 rates the chain Actively Exploited with a proof of concept available, labels only CVE-2026-120705 as actively exploited and lists watchTowr's post as its source (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-25). No victim, actor or scale is named; the project's own pages make no exploitation statement.

Eye Security's disclosure uses a different last step, CVE-2026-120704, administrator-controlled loading of an SQLite JDBC extension that gives native code execution and is fixed in the same three releases (Eye Security, 2026-11-24); on Windows the project says the extension library can load from an SMB share, so nothing needs staging on the server (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). CVE-2026-120705 echoes file contents only when a layer is published to anonymous users, and its fix reaches embedders through GeoTools 35.2, 34.6 and 33.7 (GeoServer, 2026-11-23). On a cluster, set the same GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY on every node, because the fixed releases generate a new random remember-me key at each start (watchTowr, 2026-11-25).

Update28 Nov 2026 04:50 UTCrun 2026-11-28T0355Z-intelactionsbodycvesevidenceheadlinesourcessourcing_notesummarytagstitle

CISA added CVE-2026-120705, the unauthenticated XML injection in the WFS GetFeatureById stored query, and CVE-2026-129243, the service-level authorization bypass through a prefixed service name, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-27, saying it did so on evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-11-27). CISA names no actor, victim, scale or source for that evidence, so whether it saw watchTowr's activity or its own cannot be told. The alert lists only those two GeoServer flaws, so the status of the other three still rests on watchTowr: its FAQ table now marks CVE-2026-129245, CVE-2026-129243 and CVE-2026-120705 as exploited and CVE-2026-129244 and CVE-2026-129242 as not reported, while its prose says all five are being exploited in the wild (watchTowr, 2026-11-25).

item.title: Unit 42: AI agents behind web shells in 10+ campaigns; hunt 1.4 s command gaps and ===[Title]=== headers
item.description: Unit 42 tracked more than ten campaigns between July and September 2026 in which different attackers pointed autonomous AI agents at targets in sectors including government, logistics, manufacturing and education. Every campaign began with a web shell on a vulnerable web application, after which the agent did reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement mostly with single-use scripts and no compiled implants. Unit 42 reports no new technique but measurable traces: a median gap of 1.4 seconds between commands in a subset of attacks (23.9 seconds in the human phase), section headers such as ===[Title]=== in every campaign, and 40 to 100 unique Base64 payloads per session.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Unit 42: more than ten campaigns in July to September 2026 ran autonomous AI agents from web-shell footholds on vulnerable web applications, with a command-gap median of 1.4 seconds, ===[Title]=== script headers and 40 to 100 unique Base64 payloads per session

Unit 42 tracked more than ten global campaigns between July and September 2026 in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents, against sectors including government, logistics, manufacturing, agriculture and education. Every campaign began with a web shell deployed through a vulnerable web application, typically supplied by the human operator, after which the agent did reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement; Unit 42 names no product, CVE or flaw class for the entry vectors and says the novelty was speed and efficiency, not technique (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

The traces: a median gap of 1.4 seconds between commands once an agent took over, against 23.9 seconds in the human phase of a subset of attacks; about 800 unique commands in 140 minutes in one case; section headers such as ===[Title]=== in shell commands and scripts in every campaign and step-by-step reasoning notes in more than half; 40 to 100 unique, target-tailored Base64 payloads per session; and no compiled implants, the arsenal being in most cases simple single-use scripts such as PHP web shells, PowerShell WMI backdoors and Python credential harvesters. The agents probed defences: the same find command ran on six endpoints excluding three security vendors, and one agent applied strace to the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint daemon (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

The Copy Fail exploit recurred across several organisations; in a different attack sequence an agent tried the public PwnKit and CVE-2024-1086 binaries, then wrote custom C on the target and rewrote the exploit in Python, and Unit 42 saw agents try five techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed. In one AWS case it switched to IMDSv2 token acquisition after IMDSv1 was blocked and enumerated 20 services across eight regions; in another it pushed web shells to more than 40 locations on a Windows IIS server within 26 minutes, and Unit 42 describes another agent that found a vendor's GitLab credentials on a victim's web server and tried to brute-force access to that GitLab instance, exploiting no GitLab flaw (Unit 42, 2026-11-24).

Unit 42 found no behavioural marker tying the activity to a model or framework; a command-and-control address in one campaign also hosted a CyberStrikeAI instance, from which it infers the orchestration platform (Unit 42, 2026-11-24). ReliaQuest saw a credential-gated CyberStrikeAI login page on a staging host and could not determine whether the tool played a part (ReliaQuest, 2026-10-07).

Exposure
Internet-facing web servers that host a vulnerable web application; Unit 42 does not name the applications.
Detection
In process-lineage telemetry, shells and scripts spawned through a web shell's sh -c interface in bursts seconds apart, with ===[Title]=== headers or reasoning-style comments and many unique Base64 payloads; the same enumeration command across hosts excluding security-product directories, and tracing of the endpoint-security daemon; on cloud workloads, a switch to IMDSv2 token requests after IMDSv1 is blocked.

Triage: Base64 commands and reconnaissance appear in human-operated intrusions; Unit 42's discriminators are the volume and uniqueness of payloads, the command cadence and the headers, which it says rarely appear in human-operated attacks except with pre-coded scripts.

Defender takeaway
Hunt web-server hosts for these traces, looking for volumes of single-use scripts rather than malware families, and close the web-tier entry first; enforce MFA, sign-in rate limiting and source-address restriction on services whose credentials sit on web servers, as Unit 42 advises for GitLab.

Builds on: FBI: various actors run ARTEX against many sectors, government included; Microsoft now names… · Elastic: CyberStrikeAI against AWS, six medium or low alerts joined only by source IP; alert on… · ReliaQuest: AI agents took a Tomcat server to SYSTEM in under a day through an exposed… · BACS: five confirmed AI-agent attacks in Switzerland, three on critical infrastructure…

item.title: GT13 holds Check Point management servers at 22 organisations; patching does not evict it, check audit logs
item.description: GreyNoise reports that an actor it tracks as GT13 had persistent access to at least 24 Check Point Security Management servers at 22 organisations in 17 named countries and territories (Switzerland is not among them), government among seven sectors, with confirmed activity from 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-02. The actor used a script for the SmartConsole authentication bypass CVE-2026-16232, which Check Point confirms and which has been fixed since July, to launch more than 100 management tasks that copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority. GreyNoise does not know how the actor first got in or who it is, and expects the campaign to be ongoing.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-16232 +1exploitedNATOB2

GreyNoise GT13: an unattributed actor that GreyNoise believes used LLM tooling held persistent access to at least 24 Check Point Security Management servers at 22 organisations, government among them, using CVE-2026-16232 and a Rejetto HFS relay hijacked through CVE-2026-61500

GreyNoise reports an intrusion campaign it tracks as GT13 against Check Point Security Management servers: at least 22 organisations and 24 servers, confirmed activity against the Check Point servers from 2026-10-17 to 2026-11-02 and the actor's relay observed from 2026-10-02, victims in 17 named countries and territories (Germany, Austria and France among them, Switzerland not named) and sectors including government, financial services, energy and transportation (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). GreyNoise could not determine when or how the actor first reached the Check Point servers, only that it did so before compromising the Rejetto HFS server it used as a relay; it does not attribute GT13, cannot judge motive and believes that the actor used LLM and agentic tooling (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

The actor ran a script for the SmartConsole authentication bypass CVE-2026-16232, purportedly adapted from the Metasploit module, to launch more than 100 management tasks, among them copying the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, minting a certificate and unloading security policies, which would disable the firewall (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23). Check Point confirmed the use of CVE-2026-16232 and called the flaw and its protections not new (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-24); the fixes are Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator R82.10 from Take 36, R82 from Take 118 and R81.20 from Take 158, and exploitation needs internet access to the management server with no restriction on Trusted Clients (Check Point, 2026-09-24); Check Point's disclosure table scores the flaw 9.3 and lists exploitation against a handful of customers with a specific configuration (Check Point, 2026-07-22). The relay was taken over by forging an HFS session cookie after recovering the signing key from login responses (CVE-2026-61500, HFS 3.0.0 to below 3.2.1) (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23; VulnCheck, 2026-07-13).

The actor planted an SSH key on its relay, and GreyNoise concludes from scp deliveries that each compromised device holds the matching private key; it also ran Nmap and a Chisel reverse proxy, used at least 30 Python scripts with victim-themed credential lists, and probed NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, vCenter, Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and domain controllers without any stated success. A bulk certificate task to 24 servers failed on each; GreyNoise notified victims directly or through government partners and expects the campaign to be ongoing (GreyNoise, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
Any Check Point Security Management or Multi-Domain Security Management server on R82.10, R82, R81.20 or an unsupported earlier train, below the fixed Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator, whose Trusted Clients list was unrestricted, reached from the internet or from a compromised internal host.
Detection
In management-server audit logs, SmartConsole sessions authenticated by "Password based application token", which Check Point says to treat as suspicious and check for an unrecognised administrator name or address (Check Point, 2026-09-24); script-run, certificate-management and policy-unload events; outbound SSH or scp from management servers to the relay and other non-administrator hosts; unfamiliar SSH private keys and a registration in /etc/ld.so.preload, which GreyNoise says may indicate an implant; tunnelling-tool process creation. A server patched later still needs this check, reaching back to at least early October, since the actor held persistent access and copied the internal CA.
Defender takeaway
Install the fixed Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator and restrict Trusted Clients now, then treat any server with an unexplained application-token login as a compromised management plane: review policy changes and rebuild trust where the internal CA or stored credentials left.

Builds on: Check Point patches an actively-exploited SmartConsole authentication bypass granting full… · Rejetto HFS pre-auth session forgery reaches code execution and is exploited since 2026-10-02…

item.title: BabidiGhost AI agent targeted 50+ organisations, mostly in Belgium, France, Switzerland; MFA and allow-lists held
item.description: SOCRadar reconstructs a nine-day operation (2026-11-06 to 2026-11-14) in which a low-skill French-speaking operator ran a jailbroken Hermes-based AI agent against more than 50 organisations and datasets, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland, breaching two of 14 analysed in depth and partly breaching three, the largest thefts being an insurer's customer database through an unpatched Metabase (CVE-2023-38646) and the archives of more than 13 municipalities through a weak password on a shared IT provider's storage interface, while TOTP, IP allow-listing and server-side validation stopped it. ZATAZ reports that the BlackHatSect0r handle now rents the agent and offers a bank-phishing platform that covers 28 Swiss banks; neither source names a Swiss victim.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOC2

BabidiGhost: a jailbroken Hermes-based AI agent run against more than 50 targets, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland, exported an insurer's customer database and 13 municipalities' archives through public flaws and exposures; MFA, IP allow-listing and server-side validation stopped it

SOCRadar recovered the exposed home directory of a hijacked French staging server and reconstructs a nine-day operation, 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-14, in which a low-skill French-speaking operator, BabidiGhost, typed plain-language orders to a jailbroken Hermes-based AI agent that wrote the scanners, exploits and exfiltration scripts (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20). The agent targeted more than 50 organisations and datasets, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland; of 14 analysed in depth, two were breached and three partly breached; SOCRadar says every successful intrusion used an exposed, unpatched analytics tool, a readable secret, a weak password or an unauthenticated endpoint, with no zero-day (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

An internet-facing, unpatched Metabase vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646 let the agent in; it then ran commands on the server beneath the dashboard, read cloud database credentials from the container environment, exported the customer database and planted a database trigger that relaunched its implant on every new record. A shared IT provider's storage-management interface was exposed to the internet and a weak administrator password opened it, giving 23 archives of about 8.6 GB from more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies; SOCRadar says this one server drives Belgium's share of more than half of the targets and names no Swiss municipality. Against banks the agent mapped the attack surface through certificate logs and a sign-in error oracle confirmed 48 valid corporate accounts, while a crawler swept Swiss websites for IBANs, email addresses and phone numbers. TOTP second factors, an IP allow-list and server-side business validation stopped the same agent (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Its model API key was revoked on 2026-11-14, but a PowerShell beacon and a C# backdoor posing as a Windows Update service, persisted through scheduled tasks and a Run key, kept calling home until 2026-11-15, and stolen archives had gone out through Telegram (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

ZATAZ reports that the BlackHatSect0r handle, whose toolchain SOCRadar says the agent runs, rents a jailbroken agent (ZATAZ, 2026-11-23) and offers a bank-phishing platform with templates for 81 banks in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Switzerland, 28 of them Swiss including UBS, PostFinance and Raiffeisen; ZATAZ names no Swiss victim (ZATAZ, 2026-11-23).

Exposure
The gaps used were internet-facing analytics tools, storage-management interfaces at shared IT providers, unauthenticated API routes, sign-in flows that reveal whether an account exists and secrets readable from a web application's environment (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).
Detection
Egress or proxy telemetry showing a server calling a model-provider API or the Telegram bot API without a business reason; on Windows, a Run key and scheduled tasks for a service posing as Windows Update, unexpected Defender exclusions and outbound TCP to port 8443; on PostgreSQL, triggers nobody created. SOCRadar's hunt window is 2026-11-05 to 2026-11-17, and revoking the model key did not remove deployed implants (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Triage: the Hermes Agent directory and its SOUL.md exist on every Hermes installation; they matter only when SOUL.md carries the jailbreak strings SOCRadar's rule matches (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

Defender takeaway
Patch Metabase and take analytics tools, storage-management interfaces and unauthenticated API routes off the internet, keep secrets out of runtime environments, and verify the controls that stopped the agent (TOTP, IP allow-listing, server-side validation) at the shared IT providers that hold municipal data (SOCRadar, 2026-11-20).

item.title: Kaspersky: ShadowCloud's GitDoor and GraphDoor hide C2 in GitHub and Microsoft Graph, planted via a MeshCentral agent
item.description: Kaspersky GReAT describes Operation ShadowCloud, an intrusion set identified in early 2026 that abuses the legitimate MeshCentral agent to drop two new backdoors, GitDoor and GraphDoor, with victims in Asia and Africa primarily in the government sector; the entry point is unknown. The operators sideload a loader DLL into a legitimate program beside an encrypted config.ini, and the backdoors take commands through the GitHub API (GitDoor) or Microsoft Graph and SharePoint (GraphDoor), with Ably as a further channel. Kaspersky does not attribute the activity and reports overlaps with FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle; Sophos tracks a fragment as BRONZE SANDCASTLE.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

Operation ShadowCloud: Kaspersky's GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors hide command and control in GitHub, Microsoft Graph with SharePoint, and Ably against government networks in Asia and Africa, delivered through an abused MeshCentral agent and DLL sideloading

Kaspersky GReAT describes Operation ShadowCloud, an intrusion set identified in early 2026 that abuses the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two new backdoors, with victims in Asia and Africa primarily in the government sector (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). The entry point is unknown: the first observed step is a MeshCentral agent launched inside a Taiwanese organisation, with evidence pointing to reuse of a prior infection on the network (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Through the agent the operators drop a legitimate binary, a malicious loader DLL and an encrypted payload file named config.ini, so the legitimate program loads the loader when it starts; hosts include a Sandboxie launcher, an OpenJDK launcher, a Python application and Sysinternals ZoomIt started as a service (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Sophos, which tracks the Sandboxie sideloading as BRONZE SANDCASTLE and which Kaspersky says covered a fragment of this campaign (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17), saw victims between August 2025 and August 2026 in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia and likely the Republic of Korea (Sophos, 2026-10-20).

GitDoor uses GitHub as its command channel: it opens and labels an issue through the GitHub API, writes victim data to a private repository and reads commands and plug-ins from a public one, authenticating with a personal access token (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). GraphDoor requests a token for an attacker-registered application with the client-credentials grant from Microsoft's sign-in endpoint, then writes encrypted data to files named like JavaScript source maps in a SharePoint document library through Microsoft Graph (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Both download plug-ins on demand and run shellcode in memory, among it Mimikatz and a browser-cookie stealer, with plug-ins for keylogging, screen capture and proxying through a modified Erfrp client or Ably (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17; Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). Kaspersky says it lacks sufficient information to attribute the activity and reports overlaps with the Chinese-speaking groups FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle, which on several victim systems shared staging directories with GitDoor (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Windows servers and workstations in networks that let non-browser processes reach GitHub, Microsoft's sign-in and Graph endpoints and Ably over HTTPS, and where a MeshCentral agent is not a tool the organisation deploys (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17; Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).
Detection
In endpoint inventory and process telemetry, MeshCentral agent processes and services that IT did not deploy, and a legitimate program (a Sandboxie start binary, an OpenJDK launcher, a Python host, ZoomIt) loading a DLL from the folder where an encrypted config.ini sits, as in the first instance Kaspersky shows, in system32 (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17). In network and identity telemetry, a non-browser process requesting an app-only token from Microsoft's sign-in endpoint and then writing files through Microsoft Graph to a SharePoint site outside your tenant, and a process other than a git client or CI runner calling the GitHub API to open issues, label them and write repository contents with a personal access token (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17; Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

Triage: MeshCentral is legitimate software, so the agent alone is not the signal; the signal is an agent no administrator deployed that drops a legitimate binary, a DLL and an encrypted config.ini side by side (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

Defender takeaway
Hunt now for MeshCentral agents nobody deployed and for that binary, DLL and config.ini triad, and baseline which processes on servers and workstations legitimately call GitHub, Microsoft Graph and Ably, because both backdoors hide their command channel in that traffic and Kaspersky found the entry point unknown (Kaspersky, 2026-11-17).

item.title: Rapid7: Webworm hides SoftEther VPN Bridge behind NtMonitor branding, new endpoints and an encrypted config
item.description: Rapid7 describes NtMonitor, a Windows build of SoftEther VPN Bridge 4.44 that it attributes with moderate confidence to Webworm, the China-aligned actor that ESET documented moving to European government targets in May 2026. The rebuild keeps SoftEther's function of bridging a remote network into the victim's LAN and strips its fingerprints: branding, handshake paths, the handshake watermark, the separate resource archive and the plain-text configuration are all changed, and Rapid7 found no backdoor or other added capability. Only one antivirus vendor detected the sample on VirusTotal although it has been public since January.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Webworm's NtMonitor: Rapid7 finds a custom rebuild of the SoftEther VPN Bridge that removes the open-source tool's detection fingerprints (rebranded metadata, renamed handshake endpoints, a custom handshake watermark, an embedded resource archive and an encrypted configuration), attributed with moderate confidence to the China-aligned actor that targets European governments

Rapid7 analysed what it believes is a so-far unknown custom tool, a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge version 4.44 (build 9807) that it attributes to Webworm with moderate confidence (Rapid7, 2026-11-19). Webworm is the China-aligned actor that ESET reported in May 2026 moving to European government targets and to dual-use tools such as SoftEther (ESET Research, 2026-05-20). The rebuild keeps the bridge function, which cascades a remote network into the victim's local network, and removes the fingerprints: the PE metadata and internal strings are rebranded as a network-monitoring product (inconsistently, since the service name and many registry paths still say SoftEther), the HTTP handshake endpoints get update-style names, the handshake watermark becomes a truncated PNG header so stock SoftEther peers cannot connect and the stock watermark cannot fingerprint the build, the resource archive that normally sits beside the executable is embedded in it as a PE resource, and the configuration is stored under a new name in a custom-encrypted format (Rapid7, 2026-11-19). Rapid7 found no backdoor or other added capability, concludes the actor puts stealth above capability, and says only one antivirus vendor detected the sample although it has been public since January (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).

Exposure
Windows hosts in government networks that Webworm has already compromised; Rapid7 says that in every configuration it holds the VPN is set to bridge a remote network into the local one (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Rapid7's most reliable network detection, where TLS traffic can be inspected, is a POST request to an update-themed CGI path with a JPEG content type whose body starts with a PNG file header; on hosts, look for a SoftEther VPN Bridge service that was not installed by the organisation, in particular one whose binary carries its resource archive inside itself, and for firewall rules added by such a service (Rapid7, 2026-11-19). Rapid7 calls the branding the easiest change for the actor to make next and says the endpoints and watermark can be swapped out trivially, so behaviour that is intrinsic to SoftEther matters more than any one string (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).
Defender takeaway
Government networks in Europe should treat any unmanaged SoftEther VPN Bridge, however it is named, as a persistence mechanism that bridges an outside network into theirs, and learn the tool's intrinsic behaviour, as Rapid7 recommends for the government sector (Rapid7, 2026-11-19).

item.content:encoded:
ROUTINENATOA2

Hokkaido: resident-register, support-needed and tax data of the cities of Rumoi and Iwamizawa and the town of Shintoku sat on a subcontractor's development PC infected with the K2F information stealer, which GIS Hokkaido links to the NIKKE game launcher; Rumoi's data was still there after its contract ended

Three Hokkaido municipalities disclosed on 2026-11-18 and 2026-11-19 that personal data they had handed to their contractor GIS Hokkaido was stored on a development terminal of GIS Hokkaido's subcontractor Rimgate, on which traces of the information stealer K2F were found: the terminal was infected overnight on 2 to 3 November, Rimgate found the traces on 4 November and cut it from the network, and GIS Hokkaido told the municipalities between 13 and 16 November (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19; Iwamizawa City, 2026-11-18; Shintoku Town, 2026-11-18). The data at risk is up to 71,002 resident-register records (as of February 2022) and 4,503 records of people needing support, with disability category and care level, for Rumoi, whose personal data was still on the terminal after its contract ended; 6,001 resident-register and 986 disaster-evacuation-support records for Shintoku; and up to 10,348 land parcels and 7,037 buildings of fixed-asset-tax data for Iwamizawa; none contains the national My Number and no leak or misuse is confirmed (translated from Japanese) (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19; Iwamizawa City, 2026-11-18; Shintoku Town, 2026-11-18). GIS Hokkaido told ITmedia that the PC launcher of the game NIKKE is involved and declined to say whether Rimgate staff ran the game on the work PC; ITmedia adds that a third-party tampering with that launcher, which could deliver K2F on start, became public on 5 November (translated from Japanese) (ITmedia NEWS, 2026-11-19). This is municipal public-sector data held through a supplier chain.

Exposure
Any administration whose resident, social-care or tax data went to a contractor that subcontracts, and any supplier endpoint where consumer software such as a game launcher can run next to project data; the check is which supplier terminals still hold extracts from finished projects (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19; ITmedia NEWS, 2026-11-19).
Detection
The infection path is the observable: a consumer game launcher on a workstation that holds project data, and, because K2F steals passwords and allows remote control, password-store reads by non-browser processes and unexplained remote sessions on such machines; the sources give no more specific indicator (ITmedia NEWS, 2026-11-19).
Defender takeaway
Ask each supplier and its subcontractors which of your extracts they still hold, have them delete data of finished contracts and confirm it, and keep consumer software off the machines that handle it; Rumoi's contract had ended yet its data was still on the infected terminal (Rumoi City, 2026-11-19).

Canton Basel-Landschaft: attackers took about 97,000 records from a database of work permits for cross-border commuters (permit G) in the cyberattack on the cantonal administration; the canton cannot say which records, assumes all, and names no entry point or actor

A confirmed data theft from a Swiss cantonal administration: the canton of Basel-Landschaft said on 2026-11-20 that forensic analysis showed the attackers reached a database of work permits for cross-border commuters (permit G) and took about 97,000 records for applications lodged through its online platform since 2016-11-28 (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20). It cannot establish which records were taken and assumes all, took the platform off the network, filed a criminal complaint against unknown persons and names no entry point, tool or actor (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20; Polizeiticker, 2026-11-20), after other cantonal applications had been switched off earlier in the week (Inside IT, 2026-11-20).

Exposure
Persons for whom a permit-G application was lodged, renewed or changed through the cantonal platform since 2016-11-28, and the contact persons of their employers in the canton; the database kept completed procedures too, so people whose permits ended are affected as well (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20). The canton cannot exclude that uploaded documents such as contracts or ID copies were taken but has no indication of it (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20).
Defender takeaway
An online application platform that keeps every historic procedure puts the whole archive in play when it is reached, so check how much completed data your own citizen-facing and supplier-run platforms retain; employers of cross-border commuters in the canton should expect phishing and social engineering that quotes correct personal details, because the canton warns that such messages can be built from the stolen data (Canton Basel-Landschaft, 2026-11-20).

Mitel's advisory MISA-2026-0013 of 2026-11-18 covers three flaws in the Platform component of OpenScape 4000 and OpenScape 4000 Manager, tracked by Mitel's internal ids, which the advisory page still lists without CVE ids (Mitel, 2026-11-18). MTLVULN-1785 is an unauthenticated improper-authentication flaw that gives unauthorized access and MTLVULN-1786 an unauthenticated command injection through insufficient parameter sanitization, both CVSS 3.1 10.0 with changed scope; MTLVULN-1793 is a command injection that an unauthenticated attacker with adjacent network access can use, scored 9.6 (Mitel, 2026-11-18). The CVE Program records published on 2026-11-27 map them as CVE-2026-137724 for MTLVULN-1785 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-27), CVE-2026-137721 for MTLVULN-1786 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-27) and CVE-2026-137723 for MTLVULN-1793 (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-27). Affected are OpenScape 4000 V11 R0.22 through V11 R2.11 and V10 R1.68 and earlier, and OpenScape 4000 Manager V11 R0.22 through V11 R2.11 and V10 R1.34, R1.42, R1.54 and R1.68; Mitel does not assess end-of-support releases (Mitel, 2026-11-18).

The issues are corrected in V11 R2.14, Mitel provides PLT HF5 for V11 R1.26 and a patch for V10 R0.28 to V11 R0.22 (for the Manager, V10 R1.34 to V11 R0.22), and for customers who cannot apply the fix quickly, enabling Security Mode restricted access is a workaround that prevents exploitation, with the steps in a portal-only article (Mitel, 2026-11-18). CERT-FR lists the risks as remote arbitrary code execution, remote denial of service, policy bypass and loss of integrity and confidentiality, and BSI describes an attacker who can bypass safeguards, disclose information or run arbitrary commands in the context of the system (CERT-FR, 2026-11-19; BSI, 2026-11-19). Mitel's text does not mention exploitation.

Exposure
OpenScape 4000 and OpenScape 4000 Manager at the releases above; the vulnerable component is the Platform, and the advisory does not say which of its interfaces are normally reachable (Mitel, 2026-11-18).
Detection
Unauthenticated access to the Platform component from hosts that are not administration or maintenance systems, and unexpected command execution on the platform; both follow from the improper-authentication and command-injection mechanisms, and the advisory gives no detection guidance.
Defender takeaway
Apply the fix for the release in use now; where that waits, turn on Security Mode restricted access, and read the affected range against CERT-FR's wording if the system runs R2.12 or R2.13 (Mitel, 2026-11-18; CERT-FR, 2026-11-19).

item.title: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, 3.3.14 fix seven memory flaws; Veria's Rails exploit not found yet: update the interpreter
item.description: The Ruby project released 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 on 2026-11-18 for seven memory-corruption flaws in the regexp engine and in string case conversion, three rated Critical, and says it knows of proofs of concept that reach remote code execution. Veria Labs, which found the case-conversion flaw independently (CVE-2026-132825, a one-byte heap overflow), says Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed without authentication in their default configuration and announced a code-execution proof of concept on stock Rails for 25 November 2026, which its page, blog feed and GitHub organisation did not show as released on 2026-11-27; no exploitation is reported. GitHub Enterprise Server and older GitLab branches now carry the fix. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life, and the interpreter itself, not a gem, must be updated.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-132825updatedNATOA2

Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14: seven memory-safety flaws in the regexp engine and string case conversion, three rated Critical by the project, with proofs of concept for code execution; Veria Labs says Rails and classic Sinatra are exposed by default and announces a public Rails exploit for 25 November 2026 (CVE-2026-132825, CVSS 3.1 7.4)

The Ruby project released 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 on 2026-11-18 to fix seven vulnerabilities in the regexp engine and in string case conversion, and says it is aware of proofs of concept that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution (Ruby project, 2026-11-18). NCSC.ch lists three as Critical, a one-byte heap overflow in case conversion of strings in single-byte encodings such as ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, a double free in regexp compilation and a heap overflow from an integer overflow in regexp compilation, and the rest as High or Moderate (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19); the project's advisory for the first confirms it can write one byte past the output buffer (Ruby project, 2026-11-18). Affected are Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 and 4.0.0 to 4.0.9, and Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and unfixed (Ruby project, 2026-11-18).

NCSC.ch says Rails and classic-style Sinatra are exposed to the case-conversion overflow in their default configuration (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19); watchTowr reports no exploitation as of 2026-11-19 (watchTowr, 2026-11-19). Veria Labs, which says it found the flaw independently and first demonstrated code execution, calls it Ruby2Shell, says it is reachable without authentication on Rails and classic Sinatra and that plain Rack and other frameworks are not exposed by default, and announced a proof of concept for remote code execution on stock Rails for 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix; its page, blog feed and GitHub organisation showed no release on 2026-11-27 (Veria Labs, 2026-11-19). Moritz Sanft, a co-discoverer Veria names, writes that a plain Rails application is enough to be exploitable and that OpenAI sent the Ruby maintainers working exploit proofs on 2026-11-07 (Durendal, 2026-11-19). GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.6 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.21.11 (GitHub, 2026-11-22), 3.20.13 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) and 3.19.17 (GitHub, 2026-11-22) carry the Ruby fix, although Veria's table, last changed on 2026-11-21, still shows 3.22.5 and earlier unfixed; it lists Chatwoot (4.20.1), GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject and the Discourse base image as patched, and the Ruby advisories name no product, so the vendors' own advisories decide for each (Veria Labs, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-132825 names the case-conversion overflow and is scored CVSS 3.1 7.4 with a local attack vector and high complexity (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-19); the Ruby announcement says CVE identifiers were requested and none was assigned at publication, so the other six flaws are known by GHSA id (Ruby project, 2026-11-18).

Exposure
Ruby 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0 below the fixed releases that run Rails or classic Sinatra, or any application that passes untrusted text to a case-changing method or compiles untrusted regexp patterns; the interpreter version is shown by ruby -v, and self-hosted products that bundle Ruby carry their own fix timeline (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).
Detection
Crashes, segmentation faults and abnormal restarts of Ruby application workers that coincide with requests carrying long single-byte-encoded text or unusual regexp parameters, and a shell or network tool spawned by a Ruby worker process.
Defender takeaway
Update the interpreter, not the gems, rebuild container images and restart workers, since exploit proofs exist and Veria's proof of concept may appear at any time; until then NCSC.ch's temporary measures are to avoid compiling regexps from untrusted input and, for the case-conversion flaw, to convert input to UTF-8 so the vulnerable path is not reached (NCSC.ch, 2026-11-19).

GitLab released 19.6.1, 19.5.8 and 19.4.10 on 2026-11-20 as a critical patch release for self-managed installations, with CVE-2026-132825 as its only security fix; GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched (GitLab, 2026-11-20). The fix is a patch to Ruby: official Linux packages and container images already carry it, while a self-compiled installation must rebuild Ruby 3.3.14 or 3.4.13 or a later release of the same series, and the release also covers the other flaws in the Ruby advisory (GitLab, 2026-11-20). Veria Labs' software table now lists Chatwoot 4.20.0 and earlier as fixed in 4.20.1, leaving GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 and earlier as the one product shown without a fixed release, and its proof of concept for stock Rails is still announced for 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix (Veria Labs, 2026-11-19).

item.title: PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36: FPM request smuggling to code execution; the open session flaw is fixed
item.description: The PHP project released 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and 8.6.0 on 2026-11-19 with fixes for up to 18 CVEs per branch. The most direct is CVE-2026-129289: PHP-FPM keeps unread php://input bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection, so an unauthenticated multipart request can plant a second FastCGI request and run PHP code as the worker, but only behind a front end that reuses FastCGI connections, which standard nginx and Apache setups do not. The release also fixes CVE-2026-115560, left open in October, and follow-ups to the incomplete fix for the exploited PHP2Shell flaw CVE-2026-109619; no source reports exploitation of this release's CVEs or a public proof of concept.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-129289 +7updatedNATOA2

PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36: CVE-2026-129289 lets an unauthenticated request smuggle a second FastCGI request into PHP-FPM and run PHP code when the front end reuses FastCGI connections; the release also fixes the session flaw left open in October and follow-ups to an incomplete earlier fix (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

PHP released 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, 8.2.36 and 8.6.0 on 2026-11-19, with up to 18 CVEs per branch (PHP, 2026-11-19). The most direct is CVE-2026-129289: when php://input was opened but not read to the end, PHP-FPM leaves the unread request bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection, so a malformed multipart body can place a second FastCGI request inside the first, and an unauthenticated attacker can bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker (PHP, 2026-11-19). It requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it fully; standard nginx and Apache configurations that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by the demonstrated attack (PHP, 2026-11-19).

Two session flaws close the item the October release left open (watchTowr, 2026-11-20): CVE-2026-115560, where upload-progress session data is written in one serializer format and read in another, and CVE-2026-126714, where an interrupted write by the default files handler leaves a mixed old and new session file; both end in object injection and need an object gadget chain in the application (PHP, 2026-11-19; PHP, 2026-11-19). The fix for the first disables upload progress by default (PHP, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-129481, a use-after-free of a stale session filename after an interrupted session shutdown, is in PHP's words an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619, the PHP2Shell flaw CISA has listed as exploited since 2026-10-26 (CISA, 2026-11-20), and affects PHP 8.3 and later, and CVE-2026-129182, for PHP 8.5 only, covers further scenarios after the 8.5.12 fix (PHP, 2026-11-19; PHP, 2026-11-19).

CVE-2026-129474, PHP 8.5 only, is exposed on the built-in defaults, because fatal error backtraces are on in 8.5 and the default includes arguments, and php.ini-production, which sets zend.exception_ignore_args=1, or fatal_error_backtraces=0 prevents the attack; PHP confirmed code execution on 8.5 (PHP, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-129496 needs a startup diagnostic written through a file-based error_log in a non-thread-safe build (PHP, 2026-11-19). CVE-2026-129291, an epoll use-after-free in PHP-FPM, gives root from a worker where catch_workers_output is on and the FPM master runs as root (PHP, 2026-11-19). PHP 8.5 without php.ini-production settings is exposed to CVE-2026-129474 on the defaults, when an application path enters a magic method (PHP, 2026-11-19). The session flaws need an object gadget chain in the application, and the version is shown by php -v on the host or in the container image.
Detection
In web and proxy access logs, malformed multipart/form-data bodies sent to endpoints whose application opens php://input without consuming it, followed by PHP execution that no logged request explains; in process telemetry, a shell or network tool spawned by the PHP-FPM worker, which follows from worker-level code execution.

Move the PHP runtime, not the CMS or its plugins, to the fixed build of its branch and restart PHP-FPM; where that waits, turn FastCGI connection reuse off (PHP, 2026-11-19). PHP 8.1 hosts need a newer branch for CVE-2026-129291 (PHP, 2026-11-19).
