item.title: vCenter auth bypass exploited since September; Metasploit module in public review: patch to 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 or 8.0 U3m
item.description: Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 of 2026-11-19 fixes CVE-2026-123890, an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter that needs only network access to vCenter (CVSS 3.1 9.8), with no workaround and, in Broadcom's words, an emergency change. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus actor, exploited it from early September 2026 to move from a compromised remote-support appliance to vCenter, forge administrator SAML sessions and extract domain-controller data from guest virtual disks on ESXi; Broadcom's advisory does not state exploitation. Fixed builds for this flaw are 8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200, 9.1.1.0200 and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5, but a second Directory Service bypass fixed on 2026-11-24 leaves 9.1.1.0200 and 9.0.2.0200 affected (9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m cover both). Rapid7 published a root-cause analysis and a Metasploit module is in a public pull request; vCenter 7.0 has no public fix.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-123890 +4exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-123890, VMware vCenter Server: an unauthenticated authentication bypass in the Directory Service gives an administrator session; GTIG reports the suspected China-nexus actor ARMORY CASTLE exploited it from early September, Broadcom lists no workaround; first fixed in 8.0 U3m, 9.0.2.0200 and 9.1.1.0200, with 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300 now superseding the 9.x builds (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

Broadcom's advisory VMSA-2026-0009 of 2026-11-19 fixes CVE-2026-123890, an authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service of vCenter that needs only network access (CVSS 3.1 9.8), with no workaround; it does not state exploitation (Broadcom, 2026-11-19; Broadcom, 2026-11-19). Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant say ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus actor, exploited it from early September 2026 with its BONESAW utility, in one intrusion (GTIG, 2026-11-19); BleepingComputer notes Broadcom has not confirmed it (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-19), and CISA listed the flaw as exploited on 2026-11-20 (CISA, 2026-11-20).

The cause is a session-key disclosure over DCE/RPC in the rpc_srp_verifier service on TCP 2012: the SRP key getter checks neither that the caller authenticated nor that it owns the verifier, and the RPC context handles are predictable UUIDv1 values, so an attacker needs only network access to TCP 2012 and an existing SSO principal name (Rapid7, 2026-11-24). Rapid7 chained the administrator session to a root shell on vCenter 8.0.2.00400 and describes a Metasploit module for the whole chain that sits in an open public pull request (Rapid7, 2026-11-24; Metasploit pull request, 2026-11-20). In GTIG's intrusion the actor forged administrator SAML assertions after extracting the SAML signing key, switched SSH on through the appliance management API and reached ESXi hosts, where it planted an authorized_keys entry and extracted domain data from Windows guest disks (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Fixes for this flaw: vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m and VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.5; vCenter 7.0 has no public fix (Broadcom, 2026-11-19). VMSA-2026-0011 of 2026-11-24 fixes a second Directory Service bypass, CVE-2026-123903, in 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300, so 9.1.1.0200 and 9.0.2.0200 leave it open while 8.0 U3m and 5.2.5 cover both (Broadcom, 2026-11-24).

Exposure
VCenter 7.0, 8.0, 9.0 and 9.1 before the fixed builds; the prerequisites are network access to TCP 2012 and a valid SSO principal name, and GTIG's actor reached vCenter from an internal Linux appliance, so exposure does not require an internet-facing vCenter (Rapid7, 2026-11-24; GTIG, 2026-11-19).
Detection
In network telemetry, repeated calls to operation 1 of the SRP helper interface on TCP 2012 with no RPC authentication verifier and context UUIDs that differ mainly in their timestamp fields (Rapid7, 2026-11-24), and sweeps of ports 2012, 5480 and 9080 from a Linux appliance that is not a management host (GTIG, 2026-11-19); in appliance logs, a database-transfer grant in the vmdird log, the SSH-settings request and a new local administrator in the vAPI endpoint access log and the SSH enablement itself in the appliance management log, then an SSH login followed by sudo (Rapid7, 2026-11-24); on ESXi, vpxuser or root logins, a new authorized_keys entry and a hidden directory on a VMFS volume (GTIG, 2026-11-19). A forged SAML session looks like an administrator session, and because BONESAW extracts the SAML signing key the compromise check covers SSO and local administrators, signing material and ESXi keys from early September on (GTIG, 2026-11-19).

Triage: a connection to TCP 2012 or an administrator SRP login alone proves nothing; the signal is the call pattern and log sequence above (Rapid7, 2026-11-24).

Defender takeaway
Treat the update as an emergency change and move 9.x vCenter straight to 9.1.2 or 9.0.2.0300, which cover this flaw and the second bypass; until then GTIG's hardening guidance drops inbound TCP 2012 from non-allowlisted addresses, tested first because the port carries SSO traffic (GTIG, 2026-11-19; Broadcom, 2026-11-24).

CISA listed CVE-2026-123890 as exploited on 2026-11-20 (CISA, 2026-11-20). GTIG ties the SSH enablement to the appliance management API, describes the Directory Service database being pulled through the directory service's RPC interface and the master key and credential file being read over SSH, and names no log in which those reads appear (GTIG, 2026-11-19). Broadcom lists VMware vSphere Foundation among the impacted products as well (Broadcom, 2026-11-19).

Rapid7 published its technical analysis of CVE-2026-123890 on 2026-11-24: the SRP key getter checks neither authentication nor verifier ownership and its RPC context handles are predictable, the chain reaches a root shell on vCenter 8.0.2.00400, and a Metasploit module that does the whole chain is described (Rapid7, 2026-11-24). item.title: Mandiant: COLD RELIC turns one cloud compromise into the pretext for the next; enrolled passkeys outlive password resets
item.description: Mandiant reports that COLD RELIC, the name Google Threat Intelligence Group now uses for the group formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057 (Star Blizzard), reused the staff directory and identities stolen from one US organisation in late 2025 to impersonate a contact when approaching a second in 2026. In the late-2025 case it took over a Super Admin account through push-notification fatigue, kept access with enrolled passkeys, MFA backup codes and rogue MFA devices that survived password and session resets, and exported the whole tenant; in 2026 it phished Entra ID credentials and registered a new MFA device to download one user's drive. GTIG names government officials, defense contractors and NGOs in Europe and North America as targets and says new phishing operations continued into November 2026.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

COLD RELIC: Mandiant shows the FSB-linked group reusing data stolen from one US organisation as the impersonation pretext for the next, then holding cloud tenants through MFA push fatigue and enrolled passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices that survive password and session resets

Mandiant reports a series of linked intrusions in which COLD RELIC, the name Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) now uses for the group formerly tracked as COLDRIVER and UNC4057 (also Star Blizzard, Callisto and Gossamer Bear), turned data stolen in one US organisation into the pretext for the next (GTIG, 2026-11-17). GTIG cites a US Department of Justice assessment that the group operates within Russia's FSB and names government officials, defense contractors and NGOs in Europe and North America among its targets (GTIG, 2026-11-17). In 2026 the operators approached a second US organisation over an encrypted messaging app while impersonating an employee of the first, shared phishing links that stole Entra ID credentials and tokens and sent the victim on to document lures matching the conversation, and registered a new MFA device on the account (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

In the late-2025 case the operators used the stolen credentials of a Super Admin account from a US residential proxy network close to the victim, pressed the user with MFA push notifications until one was accepted, registered a device model new to the tenant and kept access with passkeys, MFA backup codes and rogue MFA devices (GTIG, 2026-11-17). They took the whole cloud drive by mass sharing to an operator-run mailbox and by direct download, queried the admin investigation and email audit logs to check defensive visibility, viewed, modified and deleted Alert Center notifications, exported the employee list and ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout export (GTIG, 2026-11-17). Access lasted several months through OAuth mail sync to an external client and re-authentication with enrolled passkeys that survived password and session resets, and in one case a password reset without revoking sessions did not evict the operators (GTIG, 2026-11-17). They searched for credentials, personnel data and .pst archives (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Exposure
Google Workspace tenants, and Entra ID tenants that federate sign-in to Workspace as in the second case, whose privileged or staff accounts accept push, SMS or voice MFA or let users enrol passkeys, backup codes and devices without a second approval (GTIG, 2026-11-17).
Detection
In authentication logs, repeated failed logins or MFA challenges followed by a success from the same address, privileged sign-ins from residential-proxy networks that geolocate near the user, logins with a backup code, and new passkey or device registrations. In administrator audit logs, Customer Takeout creation, user-list downloads, audit-log investigation queries and Alert Center batch deletions. In Drive and OAuth logs, download spikes, external sharing to free mail providers, and authorisations of broad mail scopes to unapproved clients such as Thunderbird or Proton (GTIG, 2026-11-17). After a compromise, password changes alone are insufficient: revoke all sessions, refresh tokens and third-party OAuth permissions and remove unauthorised passkeys, backup codes and MFA devices (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Triage: a directory export, a Customer Takeout or a passkey or device enrolment by an administrator can be routine; the cues in GTIG's account are an unfamiliar device, a non-corporate or residential-proxy network, or an enrolment right after an MFA-fatigue pattern (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

Defender takeaway
Move administrators and exposed staff to FIDO2 or WebAuthn hardware keys, which GTIG says cannot be approved through fatigue or intercepted by reverse proxies, require existing-administrator or out-of-band approval for new MFA devices and passkeys, and write session and OAuth revocation into compromise playbooks (GTIG, 2026-11-17).

item.title: BundID: mass automated logins lock citizen accounts; BSI confirms; password sign-in now needs an e-mail code
item.description: On 2026-11-16 Germany's BSI confirmed automated, mass login attempts against BundID, the federal citizen account for online administrative services: failed attempts locked accounts and triggered password-reset mails, and the federal government switched off username-and-password sign-in that morning, then restored it the same afternoon with a mandatory security code by e-mail at every password sign-in, while eID and Elster sign-in stayed open. The BSI has no indication that any account was compromised; Handelsblatt, citing government circles, calls it credential stuffing.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOB2

BundID: automated mass login attempts against Germany's federal citizen accounts lock accounts; the BSI confirms the attack, password sign-in was switched off on 16 November and returned that afternoon behind an e-mail security code, and no compromise is evidenced

Germany's BSI confirmed to heise security and Handelsblatt on 2026-11-16 an IT security incident involving BundID accounts: automated, mass login attempts whose failures locked accounts, triggered automated mails and prompted account holders to reset their passwords (heise, 2026-11-16). The federal government switched off username-and-password sign-in on Monday morning for security reasons (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-16), while sign-in with the online ID card (eID) and the Elster certificate stayed possible (WEB.DE, 2026-11-16). The BSI says countermeasures it does not name repelled the attack and that it has no indication of a compromise of any account, and heise reports that locked accounts are apparently not being unlocked in bulk, so account holders must pass the password-reset flow or use another sign-in method (heise, 2026-11-16). Handelsblatt, citing government circles, describes the attack as credential stuffing, the automated replay of credentials from earlier leaks at other services (Handelsblatt, 2026-11-16). That afternoon the BundID site notice said two-factor authentication had been switched on for all accounts, with a security code by e-mail at every sign-in by username and password (Spiegel, 2026-11-16). An aggregator attributes the credential-stuffing label to the BSI, which neither heise nor Handelsblatt does (ad-hoc-news.de, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
Citizen-facing or employee-facing login portals that accept a password and lock an account after repeated failures.
Detection
Authentication logs showing a surge of failed password sign-ins spread over many usernames and sources, followed by lockout notices, password-reset mail volume and helpdesk contacts; a lockout storm is itself the alert.
Defender takeaway
The operator's containment was to switch off the password-only path while eID and other sign-in means stayed open, as heise and Handelsblatt report it, and to bring it back the same day only with an e-mail security code (Spiegel, 2026-11-16); a lockout-after-failures control turns credential stuffing into mass lockouts and reset mail even when no account is taken over, so settle that containment lever for your own portals before a run starts.
Improvement22 Nov 2026 14:53 UTCrun 2026-11-22T1407Z-auditbodyheadlinesourcessummarytitlesourcing_note

The same-day return of password sign-in now rests on the operator's own notice: on the afternoon of 2026-11-16 the BundID site said two-factor authentication had been switched on for all accounts, so every sign-in with username and password now needs a security code sent by e-mail, while sign-in with the online ID card and the Elster certificate stayed available (Spiegel, 2026-11-16).

item.title: Unit 42: TGR-STA-0049 uses QUIC C2, logon-script spread and Exchange FullAccess loops against governments
item.description: Unit 42 reports that TGR-STA-0049 (also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux and Ink Dragon) has attacked Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025, entering through unpatched Exchange and web servers, and says the group's targeting also includes governments in South America and Europe. Its new PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT implants use HTTP/3 over QUIC as the main command channel in most variants, the operators spread KUKURAT through domain logon scripts after taking a domain controller, and on Exchange they grant a compromised account FullAccess on every mailbox.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

TGR-STA-0049: Unit 42 describes the PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT implants, which use HTTP/3 over QUIC for command and control against government networks entered through unpatched Exchange servers, then spread through domain logon scripts and grant FullAccess on every mailbox

Unit 42 describes a campaign by TGR-STA-0049, also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux and Ink Dragon, against Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025, and says the group's targeting also includes government organizations in South America and Europe (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Server exploitation is the primary entry: unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers receive web shells, among them variants of ASPXSpy, Godzilla, Bysunue.aspx and Suo5, while phishing with decoy PDFs from lookalike government domains is secondary (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). The implants are two previously undocumented families: the Go-based PerfectPioneer RAT, active since July 2025 and run through DLL side-loading of a modified legitimate executable, decoy installers or phishing, and its modular C++ successor KUKURAT, deployed since March 2026, which loads at least 12 DLL modules from the command server into memory (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Unit 42 says both families use HTTP/3 over QUIC as the primary command channel, with an automatic HTTP/2 fallback in the PerfectPioneer variant it analyzes, separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 builds of KUKURAT, and two PerfectPioneer variants, RatAAkk-tt and PerfectRat, that rely on HTTP/2 alone, and that some firewalls and inspection engines handle QUIC less well than TCP traffic (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Two of the six PerfectPioneer variants, Pioneer and rat_http3_cc, carry a built-in blocklist that stops operators running noisy or destructive commands, and KUKURAT generates synthetic network, registry and file activity as camouflage (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).

After taking a domain controller, the operators installed malicious domain logon scripts, so each user's logon pulled KUKURAT; they also used PsExec, WMI and WinRM (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). Credentials came from LSASS dumps taken with rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll by ordinal rather than by the MiniDump name, from DCSync, and from Mimikatz, ProcDump, SharpDPAPI and SAM and SYSTEM hive dumps (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). On Exchange, the operators first listed accounts holding the ApplicationImpersonation role and, when none was found, ran a hidden PowerShell loop that granted a compromised account FullAccess on every mailbox (Unit 42, 2026-11-16). The exfiltration targeted pdf, docx, xlsx and png files whose names suggest international relations and internal political affairs (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).

Exposure
On-premises Exchange and other web servers that are unpatched and internet-facing, and Active Directory domains in which an attacker with domain controller access can edit logon scripts in SYSVOL or Group Policy.
Detection
Egress telemetry for outbound UDP 443 (QUIC) from servers that do not browse, since Unit 42 advises logging or blocking it so traffic falls back to TCP, paired with proxy and TLS egress telemetry because the HTTP/2-only variants and the KUKURAT HTTP/2 build never use UDP 443; SYSVOL and Group Policy change audit plus endpoint alerts on an uncommon startup process running under a domain user SID at logon, which raised an alert in Unit 42's telemetry; process events for rundll32 loading comsvcs.dll with an ordinal argument; and Exchange audit of ApplicationImpersonation role holders and of Add-MailboxPermission loops that grant FullAccess across all mailboxes (Unit 42, 2026-11-16).
Defender takeaway
Patch or isolate internet-facing Exchange and web servers first, then check domain logon scripts, ApplicationImpersonation holders and mailbox permissions, and decide whether servers need outbound UDP 443 at all.

Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians: on 2026-11-12 a guest-pushed batch file ran on a technician's client with no prompt and installed a rogue ScreenConnect client within about nine seconds, while attacker guests were making 688,000 run-file requests on 42 MSP servers between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16. Updating the server does not fix it; every technician host client must be on 26.6.5 or later.

Huntress confirmed exploitation of CVE-2026-84869 against MSP technicians in a campaign it separates from the crypto-exchange-named decoy sessions it reported on 2026-11-13, and it describes the SCKit malware as appearing to leverage a vulnerable server-side extension, not to exploit this flaw directly (Huntress, 2026-11-16). On 2026-11-12 a technician at one MSP joined a blank-named Access session on the MSP's server and the host client ran a batch file the guest had pushed, with no prompt; within about nine seconds a hidden PowerShell relaunch, a curl download and an administrative-image unpack of an MSI ended with a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to an attacker relay on port 8041 (Huntress, 2026-11-16). Huntress read the delivery side from server databases: between 2026-10-20 and 2026-11-16 attacker guests made 688,000 run-file requests for update.bat-style files from 29 source addresses on 42 MSP servers, repeating them in case a technician joined, and Huntress assesses with high confidence that the spray operator and the relay operator are the same (Huntress, 2026-11-16). In October an attacker also joined three real customer support sessions as an extra guest and asked the technician's client to run a path-traversal file into the Startup folder; two of the three technicians were on vulnerable Windows clients and the Mac client failed (Huntress, 2026-11-16).

The vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine, so updating the server alone does not close it, and Huntress saw many technicians on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after 26.6.5 shipped (Huntress, 2026-11-16). Server-side, Huntress points to guest-originated file-run events (RanFiles, EventType 85, or SentFiles, 86) in App_Data\Session.db, read from a copy, that overlap an open host connection; on workstations it points to the ScreenConnect client running batch or script files from its Temp folder, and to any client whose command line names a relay the organisation does not own (Huntress, 2026-11-16).

The FBI's FLASH of 2026-11-13 says a variety of actors have used ARTEX since at least August against sectors including government, with more than 1,600 exposed consoles in early November. The FBI's FLASH of 2026-11-13 (TLP:CLEAR) adds a US authority's account of ARTEX use. It says a variety of malicious actors have used the framework since at least August 2026 against organisations in financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal services, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours (FBI, 2026-11-13). The original repository was withdrawn on 2026-10-08, but forks, archived copies and a commercial version keep the framework available, and researchers identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November (FBI, 2026-11-13). The FBI says ARTEX excels at finding and exploiting peripheral systems that get less security attention: partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee applications, legacy services and third-party integrations (FBI, 2026-11-13).

The FBI's table of observed activity lists these further steps. Initial access came through unsigned SAML assertions, XXE, SSRF, anonymous file upload, hard-coded administrator passwords in single-page-application JavaScript bundles, stolen VPN configurations and leaked credentials, cross-account cloud trust abused from an external partner tenant, and compromised third-party vendor credentials used across trusted B2B federation. Persistence used JSP and PHP web shells (one route was MySQL log poisoning), Kudu administrative APIs to run commands, and credentials added to existing OAuth applications. For privilege escalation and internal discovery the agents used Kerberoasting, DCSync, resource-based constrained delegation abuse and a cloud metadata query through XXE, ran iterative PowerShell enumeration against domain controllers (over 110,000 Active Directory objects), read LAPS passwords and inventoried Windows hosts without a particular EDR sensor; attempted lateral movement to domain controllers by pass-the-ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay and pass-the-hash was blocked by endpoint protection. Theft preparation used database queries, mass blob reads, custom boot scripts via EC2 instances and new 100 GB volumes, with command output sent to rotating webhook endpoints, and command and control ran through residential proxies, Tor, Chisel and SoftEther (FBI, 2026-11-13).

Telemetry the FBI lists: unexpected outbound calls to LLM API endpoints (to be read alongside other suspicious activity), high-frequency sequential enumeration against login and search endpoints, Azure Resource Manager deployment-validation dry runs across many resource types, IAM permission tests with DryRun flags and sub-second test blob writes and deletes, credential additions to applications and service principals in the Entra audit log, and .aspx or .jsp files in unexpected web-application paths (FBI, 2026-11-13). Its recommendations: inventory every internet-facing application including the peripheral ones named above, restrict Kudu/SCM endpoints, cloud administration, hypervisor and backup interfaces to trusted networks or dedicated administrative paths, and disable basic publishing authentication where it is not required. For every Microsoft 365 tenant where an affected ConnectWise application is or was authorised, it asks for a review by application ID of activity from at least 2026-10-01 and says not to delete the enterprise application before evidence is preserved (FBI, 2026-11-13).

Open finding: ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration →

ANSSI's second REACTIV report of 2026-11-12 counts 64 further breaches, five at ministries, says all exploit the weaknesses already listed and names the reuse of stolen secrets as the technique, with new cases of an SMS second factor validated by the attacker and IDOR flaws combined with infostealer credentials.

ANSSI's second REACTIV situation report, published on 2026-11-12, counts 64 new data breaches brought to its attention since the first report of 2026-09-30, five of them at ministries or bodies under their supervision, with a significant fall in breaches detected or claimed at ministry level; it says all of them exploit weaknesses already named in September and gives the reuse of stolen secrets to reach ministry applications as the technique, which lets attackers extract the data legitimately (translated from French) (ANSSI, 2026-11-12). The new cases it describes: stolen technical accounts reused against a foreign-ministry library portal after a server compromise; an IDOR flaw in the payment API of a public registration portal for the hunting-licence exam, exposing more than a thousand people; an agent's France Travail account compromised with the SMS second factor validated, with the data of more than 60,000 agents and professionals claimed on a forum; and partner-account credentials from infostealers without two-factor authentication, combined with an IDOR flaw on a URL exposing file identifiers, which let attackers extract close to 1.2 million files from the CAF's VACAF service in three days. Education nationale is now put at 25 of 30 académies, with lateral movement over the interministerial network (ANSSI, 2026-11-12). ANSSI's recommendations are renewing compromised or suspect secrets first, systematic strong authentication, strict control of privileged accounts and tighter filtering to prevent exfiltration (ANSSI, 2026-11-12).

Open finding: ANSSI's REACTIV situation reports on French state data breaches: 99 since 1 August in the first, driven by Metabase CVE-2026-72898, infostealer credentials without MFA, IDOR flaws and supplier rebound, and 64 more in the second, which names the reuse of stolen secrets as the one recurring technique →

item.title: Group-IB: DarkLunnen's FortiOS chain leaves a 'service' super_admin; Swiss FortiGates are scan targets only
item.description: Group-IB found an open directory on a Latvian server that documents more than 14 months of operations against Europe by an operator it tracks as DarkLunnen and links to no known actor: a modified public exploit for FortiOS CVE-2024-55591 that creates an administrator named service with super_admin privileges, among other tools. Group-IB recovered a list of 4,725 Swiss FortiGate scanning targets, which it says does not confirm vulnerability or exploitation, and restic commands that accessed an S3 backup repository at a Swiss domain in May and June 2025, without naming an organisation or confirming success.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLEexploitedNATOB2

DarkLunnen: Group-IB's exposed operator directory shows mass exploitation of FortiOS CVE-2024-55591 that plants a 'service' super_admin account, a 4,725-target Swiss FortiGate scan list and restic access to an S3 backup repository at a 'Swiss domain'; Group-IB does not confirm any Swiss victim

Group-IB reports that in late July 2026 it found an open directory on a Latvian server that held the operator's /root/ directory, 457 files of which 35 were recovered, and documents more than 14 months of operations against Europe by an operator it tracks as DarkLunnen; Group-IB links it to no known actor and does not establish nationality or state affiliation (Group-IB, 2026-11-11). The main campaign used a modified watchTowr proof of concept for FortiOS CVE-2024-55591, designed to create a backdoor super-admin account named service (Group-IB, 2026-11-11); the recovered results list about 600 devices in Turkey (hospitals, industry and municipalities), 16 in Ukraine, 14 in Azerbaijan and 1 in Algeria, and a stolen FortiGate configuration from a Romanian organisation carried the same account and yielded 10 cleartext VPN passwords (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).

The Swiss content is thin. Group-IB recovered a list of 4,725 FortiGate scanning targets for Switzerland and says such lists identify scanning targets but do not confirm vulnerability or successful exploitation; a table of additional operations also lists restic commands with AWS credentials accessing an S3 repository at a Swiss domain in May and June 2025, with production snapshots enumerated, and the report names no organisation and says that for several operations the evidence is limited to recorded commands (Group-IB, 2026-11-11). Fortinet's advisory FG-IR-24-535 lists FortiOS 7.0.0 through 7.0.16 and FortiProxy 7.2.0 through 7.2.12 and 7.0.0 through 7.0.19 as affected, fixed in 7.0.17, 7.2.13 and 7.0.20, names FortiOS 7.2, 7.4, 7.6 and 6.4 as not affected and offers disabling the HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface as the workaround (Fortinet PSIRT, 2025-01-14).

Exposure
A FortiOS 7.0 device below 7.0.17, or a FortiProxy below its fixed release, whose HTTP/HTTPS administrative interface was ever reachable from the internet; a device exposed while vulnerable can carry an account that patching does not remove (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).
Detection
In FortiGate event logs, an administrator named service with the super_admin profile, any unexplained administrator or local user, and super_admin logins or account creation through the jsconsole interface, which Fortinet lists among its indicators; in VPN logs, logins with accounts whose secrets sat in an exposed configuration (Group-IB, 2026-11-11).
Defender takeaway
Hunt for the account on patched devices too, assume the configuration was read on a device that was exposed while vulnerable and rotate the VPN user passwords, administrator passwords, IPsec pre-shared keys and LDAP or RADIUS credentials it stored, review VPN logs and enforce MFA, and enable private data encryption, which is off by default (Group-IB, 2026-11-11); no source says that a Swiss organisation was compromised.

item.title: WFX Phantom: stolen GitHub tokens push a CI stealer; cloud persistence meant to survive rotation; check for probe PRs
item.description: StepSecurity and Aikido report that from 2026-11-10 an attacker uses stolen GitHub tokens, not a GitHub Actions bug, to open probe pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes" and then push a stealer script into workflows, CI scripts or npm hooks where the token's permissions allow, taking Actions secrets, runner memory and cloud credentials, planting AWS and Azure persistence and deleting the workflow runs. Counts differ by lab and time (more than 63,000 probes; at least 1,835 repositories where the payload ran); how the tokens were obtained is unknown, and no Swiss victim is named.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

WFX Phantom: stolen GitHub tokens push a CI secret stealer into repositories from 2026-11-10, steal Actions secrets, runner memory and cloud tokens, plant AWS and Azure persistence designed to outlast rotation and delete the workflow runs; StepSecurity counts more than 63,000 probe pull requests

StepSecurity reports that from 2026-11-10 an attacker uses stolen GitHub tokens of real developer and bot accounts, as a developer would, not a bug in GitHub Actions, to push a CI secret stealer into repositories those tokens can write to (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). It first opens a pull request titled "docs: dependency audit notes" from a branch named wfx-docs that only proves write access; StepSecurity counts more than 63,000 such probes by 2026-11-12 (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12), Aikido, which tracks the campaign as wfx-loot, counts 4,837 compromised accounts and at least 1,835 repositories where the payload ran, and Endor Labs counts 8,926 infected repositories (Aikido, 2026-11-12; Endor Labs, 2026-11-12); BleepingComputer reports that the compromised accounts included those of the US General Services Administration and the French government (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

Where the token's permissions and the repository's setup let it run, the attacker pushes a script of about 1,500 lines through an edit to an existing workflow or CI shell script, a new workflow on a short-lived branch or a hidden script that an npm hook runs, and the script collects every Actions secret, the job token, the memory of the runner worker process and credential files for the major clouds and registries, then uses the job's OIDC token to open AWS, GCP and Azure sessions (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). It plants persistence meant to outlast rotation, a rewritten AWS role trust policy with new access keys and federated identity credentials on Azure applications, sends the archive over HTTP and from 2026-11-12 through a Telegram bot, and within about a minute pushes a revert commit and deletes the workflow run, leaving a gap in the run numbers that StepSecurity calls the most reliable sign the stealer ran (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). How the tokens were obtained is not known: some probes came through the Fly.io GitHub App, and StepSecurity has no evidence of a breach of Fly.io (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12). BleepingComputer's report of Aikido's findings gives the same probe title and start date (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
Any account or bot with write access to repositories you own or build from whose token may be exposed (a personal access token, an OAuth grant, a GitHub App user token), and any build with cloud OIDC trust or long-lived secrets; bots that bypass branch protection raise the risk (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).
Detection
In source-control data, pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes", branches named wfx-docs and commits since 2026-11-10 with the messages "ci: refresh build cache", "ci: restore", "ci: cleanup", "chore: add ci helper" or "chore: add dependency audit workflow", and in CI run history a gap in the run numbers right after one; in AWS and Azure audit logs, changes to role trust policies, newly created access keys and federated credentials named wfx-ci (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).

Triage: a probe pull request alone shows that the account that opened it is compromised, even if nothing else happened; the payload probably ran where a commit with one of those messages is paired with a deleted run (StepSecurity, 2026-11-12).

Defender takeaway
Treat the account behind any probe or payload commit as compromised and revoke its tokens; where the payload ran, rotation is not enough because the persistence is designed to outlast it, and Endor Labs says secrets rotated after the first wave were likely stolen again in 1,838 repositories (Endor Labs, 2026-11-12).

Builds on: GhostAction: fake security workflows now harvest whole git histories; rotating Actions secrets…
